title: A Phase 2 Trial Evaluating the Immunogenicity and Safety of an mRNA-Based Seasonal Influenza Vaccine Candidate Encoding Hemagglutinin and Neuraminidase.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to evaluate the immunogenicity and safety of an mRNA-based vaccine candidate targeting both hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) in seasonal influenza viruses, as current vaccines primarily target HA and may not provide broad protection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A randomized phase 2 trial was conducted in two age cohorts: younger adults (18–64 years) and older adults (65–85 years). Participants received either an mRNA vaccine formulation or a licensed seasonal influenza vaccine as the comparator.
analysis.methods: The study assessed Day-29 hemagglutination inhibition (HI) and neuraminidase inhibition (NI) responses as primary and secondary endpoints, respectively, with virus neutralization as the tertiary endpoint. Safety and reactogenicity were also evaluated as secondary endpoints.
analysis.main_results: In part 1, HI responses against A/H1N1 and A/H3N2 were similar or higher after FLUm3HA-3NA than after comparator vaccination in both age groups. For B/Victoria, HI responses were lower or similar in younger adults and similar or higher in older adults. In part 2, HI responses were similar or higher with FLUm3HA-3NA versus comparators for A/H1N1 and A/H3N2, and lower for B/Victoria in both age groups. NI titers were higher for all three strains with FLUm3HA-3NA versus comparators, and neutralizing titers were similar or higher for A/H1N1 and A/H3N2 and similar for B/Victoria.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that the vaccine induced immune responses to both HA and NA, with an acceptable safety profile, and noted that the results support further development, particularly focusing on improving the immune response to the flu B virus.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that targeting both HA and NA in an mRNA vaccine could enhance protection against seasonal influenza viruses, potentially leading to more effective vaccines that address the limitations of current HA-only vaccines.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited to two age groups and did not evaluate long-term efficacy or immune persistence. The evidence is moderate, as the results are based on immunogenicity and safety assessments without long-term follow-up or broader population data.

analysis.summary_en: This phase 2 trial evaluated an mRNA-based vaccine candidate targeting both hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) in seasonal influenza viruses. The study involved 411 younger adults and 422 older adults, comparing different mRNA formulations with licensed vaccines. The vaccine induced immune responses to both HA and NA, with higher neuraminidase inhibition titers than comparators. HI responses were similar or higher for A/H1N1 and A/H3N2 but lower for B/Victoria. Safety was acceptable, and the results support further development, particularly to enhance B/Victoria immune responses. The study's limitations include its focus on two age groups and lack of long-term efficacy data, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

title: Seasonal influenza vaccination among healthcare workers in Lebanese hospitals: determinants of uptake post-COVID-19 pandemic and economic crisis

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess self-reported influenza vaccination uptake among healthcare workers (HCWs) in Lebanese hospitals during 2023–2024, comparing it with pre-pandemic 2018–2019 uptake, and identified factors associated with non-vaccination. HCWs are at increased risk of acquiring and transmitting influenza.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A cross-sectional survey was conducted from April to July 2024 among HCWs from 14 public and private hospitals across multiple regions of Lebanon.
analysis.methods: The survey assessed influenza vaccination status, free institutional vaccine provision, awareness, attitudes, and COVID-19 vaccine-related perceptions. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors independently associated with non-vaccination in 2023–2024.
analysis.main_results: Among 391 participants, self-reported influenza vaccination uptake was lower in 2023–2024 than in 2018–2019 (29.9% vs 60.5%, p < 0.0001). Free institutional vaccine provision was also lower (39.6% vs 70.1%, p < 0.0001), and 19.2% were willing to pay out of pocket.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Higher odds of non-vaccination were observed among HCWs aged <30 years, non-physicians, those without free institutional vaccine provision, those with unfavorable influenza vaccination attitudes, and those with moderate-to-high COVID-19 vaccine-related hesitancy.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Restoring free workplace-based vaccination and addressing COVID-19 vaccine-related hesitancy may improve uptake in resource-constrained healthcare settings.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its cross-sectional design, which cannot establish causality, and the potential for self-report bias. The sample size and regional diversity may affect generalizability.

analysis.summary_en: This study found that influenza vaccination uptake among Lebanese healthcare workers decreased significantly from 2018–2019 to 2023–2024, with younger HCWs and those with unfavorable attitudes being less likely to vaccinate. Improving access and addressing hesitancy could enhance future uptake.

title: Genomic investigation of an Influenza A(H3N2) subclade K outbreak in a secondary school in Burundi, 2026

analysis.research_question_and_background: Severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) are an important public health concern, particularly in settings where identification of the causative pathogen can be challenging. Testing of patients with unexplained SARI and characterization of causative pathogens also is seen as an important pillar of emerging disease preparedness.
analysis.study_design_and_population: In January 2026, an increase in respiratory illness cases was reported in a secondary school in Bujumbura, Burundi, raising concerns about a possible resurgence of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). However, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) testing of symptomatic individuals was negative, suggesting the involvement of another respiratory pathogen.
analysis.methods: To identify the causative agent, nasopharyngeal samples collected from symptomatic students were investigated using targeted viral enrichment sequencing. Eight SARS-CoV-2-negative samples were sequenced using the Illumina Viral Surveillance Panel v2 on the iSeq 100 platform. Sequencing reads were quality-checked and analysed for viral identification, followed by genome reconstruction, clade assignment, and phylogenetic analysis of the identified viruses.
analysis.main_results: Influenza A virus (IAV) was detected in seven of the eight analyzed samples. Four samples yielded near-complete IAV genomes, allowing detailed genomic characterization. All characterized genomes were identified as Influenza A(H3N2) subclade K, representing the first genomic detection and characterization of this subclade in Burundi. Phylogenetic analysis showed that Burundian sequences clustered into two distinct groups, suggesting the circulation of at least two viral lineages during the outbreak.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The identification of different viral lineages highlights the value of genomic approaches to complement routine laboratory testing and support outbreak investigation and respiratory pathogen surveillance in Burundi. This study provides the first genomic characterization of Influenza A(H3N2) subclade K in Burundi.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the need for genomic surveillance to better understand the epidemiology of influenza in Burundi and support outbreak response strategies. They also emphasize the importance of targeted viral enrichment sequencing in identifying causative agents when initial tests are inconclusive.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the small sample size and the focus on a single outbreak setting. The evidence is moderate, as the results are based on genomic analysis of a limited number of samples from a specific location and time period.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated an outbreak of respiratory illness in a secondary school in Bujumbura, Burundi, in January 2026, where initial concerns about a resurgence of COVID-19 were raised. However, SARS-CoV-2 testing was negative, prompting further investigation into other pathogens. Using targeted viral enrichment sequencing, the study identified Influenza A virus (IAV) as the causative agent, with seven of eight samples testing positive. Four samples provided near-complete genomes, all classified as Influenza A(H3N2) subclade K, marking the first genomic detection of this subclade in Burundi. Phylogenetic analysis revealed two distinct viral lineages circulating during the outbreak. The study highlights the utility of genomic approaches in outbreak investigations, especially when routine testing is limited. The findings suggest the importance of enhancing surveillance for influenza in Burundi and underscore the value of targeted sequencing in identifying pathogens in complex outbreaks. However, the study's small sample size and limited geographic scope may affect the generalizability of the results.

title: Developing and benchmarking one health genomic surveillance tools for influenza A virus in wastewater

analysis.research_question_and_background: Influenza A viruses (IAV) remain a persistent One Health threat, and whole-genome sequencing from wastewater offers a promising surveillance tool.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We benchmark four targeted enrichment methods suited for multi-subtype whole-genome IAV sequencing including custom and off-the-shelf methods.
analysis.methods: Across all four sequencing methods, two wastewater matrices, and most spike-in and endogenous virus targets, ultrafiltration-based virus concentration consistently outperforms large-volume direct extraction.
analysis.main_results: In real wastewater samples, our custom probe panel recovers whole-genome signals from circulating H1N1, H3N2, H5N1, including validated H5N1 2.3.4.4b reads in samples where dPCR detection is limited.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Our custom HA tiled-amplicon panel is sensitive, fast, and cost-effective, making it suitable for monitoring low-abundance seasonal variants of known subtypes, although its reliance on conserved and intact primer-binding sites limits primer design to fewer subtypes.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Together, these benchmarking comparisons and custom panels provide needed information for implementing IAV genomic sequencing in routine wastewater surveillance.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Probe-capture methods are generally more costly and labor-intensive than amplicon methods.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to develop and benchmark genomic surveillance tools for influenza A virus (IAV) in wastewater. The researchers evaluated four targeted enrichment methods, including custom and off-the-shelf approaches, to determine their effectiveness in sequencing low-abundance IAV subtypes. They found that ultrafiltration-based virus concentration outperformed large-volume direct extraction across multiple methods and wastewater matrices. Their custom probe panel successfully recovered whole-genome signals from H1N1, H3N2, and H5N1 in real wastewater samples, although it is limited to fewer subtypes due to its reliance on conserved primer-binding sites. The study highlights the potential of these methods for routine wastewater surveillance of seasonal IAV variants, while noting that probe-capture methods are more costly and labor-intensive. The findings suggest that tailored approaches can enhance the sensitivity and efficiency of IAV genomic monitoring in wastewater, though limitations in method design and cost must be considered.

title: Birth Cohort Effects in Adults Associated With Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 Vaccine Effectiveness.

analysis.research_question_and_background: In 2023-2024 influenza season, adults in the 1957-1985 birth cohort had the lowest vaccine effectiveness (VE) against A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses compared to other age groups, including those in the 1986-2005 birth cohort. analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved collecting acute and convalescent sera from adults (1986-2005 and 1957-1985 birth cohorts) during 2023-2024. Hemagglutination inhibiting (HI) and binding antibodies were assessed against representative A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses and hemagglutinin antigens.
analysis.methods: Acute and convalescent sera were collected from adults (1986-2005 and 1957-1985 birth cohorts) during 2023-2024.
analysis.main_results: A(H1N1)pdm09-infected cases in the 1957-1985 birth cohort had significantly lower HI antibodies in the acute sera against circulating A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses than 1986-2005 birth cohort. Antibody landscape analysis revealed that these patients born in 1957-1985 with the lowest VE were likely primed with USSR/77-like A(H1N1) viruses.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: HI antibody levels in the acute sera were associated with protection against influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 infection. The study suggests low vaccine immunogenicity in the 1957-1985 birth cohort, which could explain the observed birth cohort effect of low VE.

analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study design limitations include the observational nature of the study and the potential for confounding factors. Nonetheless, the robust antibody responses in vaccinated cases in the 1957-1985 birth cohort suggest low vaccine immunogenicity, which is a significant finding. The evidence strength is moderate.

analysis.summary_en: The study investigated A(H1N1)pdm09 antibody levels in sera from adults in different birth cohorts to explain the low vaccine effectiveness observed in the 1957-1985 cohort. The findings suggest low vaccine immunogenicity in this cohort, which could be addressed by improving vaccine design.

title: T cell Cyp27b1 promotes granzyme B expression and antiviral host defense in a mouse model of H1N1 influenza A virus infection

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the role of immune cell-derived 1,25(OH) 2 D in host resistance to influenza infection, building on the background that immune cells express vitamin D receptors and the CYP27B1 enzyme, which are involved in producing the VDR ligand, 1,25(OH) 2 D.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used a mouse model of H1N1 influenza A virus infection, examining various mouse strains including wild type (WT) littermates, whole-body Cyp27b1 knockout (Cyp27b1 KO) mice, mice lacking renal 1,25(OH) 2 D production (double intronic (DI)KO), mice with T cell-specific deletion of Cyp27b1 (T-Cyp27b1 KO), and mice with T cell-specific deletion of Vdr (T-Vdr KO).
analysis.methods: Mice were infected with mouse-adapted H1N1 influenza A virus to determine the role of CYP27B1 in host resistance, with specific attention to the effects of Cyp27b1 deletion in different mouse strains.
analysis.main_results: Whole body Cyp27b1 KO mice developed severe influenza A virus disease, including infection-induced mortality, compared to WT littermates. T cell-specific Cyp27b1 KO mice showed increased respiratory distress and lethargy compared to WT littermates.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that immune cells, particularly T cells, may produce 1,25(OH) 2 D locally to support CD8+ T cell responses to influenza A virus infection, highlighting a novel role for CYP27B1 in antiviral host defense.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results provide insights into the local regulation of 1,25(OH) 2 D production in immune cells during influenza infection, which could inform future studies on immune modulation and potential therapeutic strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a mouse model, and the evidence is moderate as it does not fully address the role of 1,25(OH) 2 D in human influenza infections.

Whole-body Cyp27b1 knockout mice showed severe disease, while T cell-specific knockout mice exhibited increased respiratory distress and lethargy. Oral treatment with 1,25(OH) 2 D did not fully protect Cyp27b1 KO mice, suggesting local production is critical. The findings emphasize the importance of defining mechanisms regulating local 1,25(OH) 2 D production in immune cells. However, the study is limited to a mouse model, and its implications for human influenza remain speculative.

title: Bat-borne influenza A H9N2 virus shows species-specific replication and transmission

analysis.study_design_and_population: The study compared the susceptibility of two pteropodid bat species, Rousettus aegyptiacus and Eidolon helvum, and also assessed pigs and quails following intranasal inoculation with bat H9N2.
analysis.methods: The researchers intranasally inoculated the animals and assessed viral replication, shedding, and transmission through examination of viral RNA levels in various tissues and observation of clinical signs.
analysis.main_results: Rousettus aegyptiacus showed only low-level viral replication and shedding, largely restricted to the upper respiratory tract, and did not show transmission to contact bats. In contrast, both juvenile and adult Eidolon helvum showed high-level viral replication and shedding in the upper respiratory tract, with efficient and early transmission to contact bats.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrate marked differences in susceptibility to bat H9N2 between the two fruit bat species tested and identify Eidolon helvum as a highly susceptible host capable of rapid and efficient transmission.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results highlight the importance of understanding the host range of bat-borne H9N2 IAV for surveillance and risk assessment, particularly in identifying potential reservoir hosts and mixing-vessel species.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to in vivo experiments with a small number of animals and does not include long-term monitoring or broader host species, but the evidence is strong due to direct observations of replication, shedding, and transmission.

The study's limitations include a small sample size and focus on specific animal models, but the evidence is strong based on direct observations of viral behavior.

analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The direct measurement of fitness flux offers a transparent, frequency-based alternative to mutational proxies for tracking and anticipating viral adaptation. title: Matrix Metalloproteinase-8 Deficiency Alters the Balance Between Viral Clearance and Immunopathology in H1N1 Infection.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Matrix metalloproteinase-8 (MMP-8) regulates inflammatory responses, but its contributions to the pathogenesis of influenza A viral (IAV) disease are not known.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved H1N1-infected wild-type (WT) mice and Mmp-8-/- mice, with plasma MMP-8 levels measured in subjects infected with H1N1 or seasonal IAV.
analysis.methods: MMP-8 levels were elevated in the lungs of H1N1-infected WT mice and localized to airway epithelial cells, macrophages, and polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs).
analysis.main_results: H1N1-infected Mmp-8-/- mice exhibited lower mortality and reduced lung viral burdens, but developed more severe lung injury than WT mice. Gene expression profiling revealed enhanced necroptosis and an exaggerated immune response in the lungs of infected Mmp-8-/- mice.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Infected Mmp-8-/- mice had increased airway epithelial necroptosis with higher pulmonary levels of Type I interferons (IFNs), and increased frequencies of Class II MHC molecule-expressing macrophages and CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, and higher levels of some Th1 cytokines. MMP-8 may represent a host-response target in severe influenza infection, although therapeutic strategies targeting MMP-8 will need to balance enhanced viral clearance against the risk of increased lung immunopathology.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that Mmp-8 deficiency is associated with restricted influenza virus spread and increased lung injury, accompanied by enhanced Type I IFN-associated necroptotic signaling and augmented antiviral immune responses. MMP-8 may be a potential target for therapeutic intervention in severe influenza infection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the use of a single influenza strain and the absence of direct clinical validation of MMP-8 as a biomarker or therapeutic target. The findings suggest a complex interplay between MMP-8 and immune responses in influenza pathogenesis, but further research is needed to confirm these results in larger cohorts and in human studies.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the role of MMP-8 in H1N1 influenza infection, finding that MMP-8 deficiency reduces viral spread but increases lung injury and immune responses. The findings suggest MMP-8 as a potential therapeutic target, but further clinical validation is needed.

title: Protective Effects of Influenza B Neuraminidase Antibodies Against Symptomatic Influenza Virus Infection.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Influenza vaccines are designed to induce hemagglutinin-inhibiting (HAI) antibodies rather than neuraminidase-inhibiting (NAI) antibodies; therefore, NAI antibodies' protective effects need further investigation.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Neuraminidase-inhibiting antibodies' protective effects, independent of HAI antibodies, have been demonstrated for influenza A viruses, but not influenza B viruses (IBVs).
analysis.methods: Employing H6NB reassortant virus targets, we evaluated NAI antibodies' protective effects against IBV in sera from a prospective influenza vaccine effectiveness study among healthcare personnel (HCP) in Israel.
analysis.main_results: Laboratory-confirmed IBV infection was recorded in 64/262 HCP and influenza vaccination in 187/262 HCP.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Matched NAI and HAI antibody titers from baseline and postvaccination sera were analyzed for the 2017-2018 influenza season.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Each 2-fold rise in NAI antibody titers reduced the hazard of symptomatic infection by 42% (95% CI: 36%-48%) against B/Phuket and 23% (95% CI: 13%-33%) against B/Brisbane, adjusting for HAI titers.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Neuraminidase-inhibiting antibodies were a strong correlate of protection against symptomatic IBV infection, with protective effects independent of those from HAI antibodies.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the protective effects of neuraminidase-inhibiting (NAI) antibodies against symptomatic influenza B virus (IBV) infection, highlighting a gap in current vaccine design that focuses on hemagglutinin-inhibiting (HAI) antibodies. The research was conducted among healthcare personnel (HCP) in Israel using sera from a prospective vaccine effectiveness study. NAI and HAI antibody titers were quantified against specific IBV strains, and the results showed that NAI titers were significantly higher in vaccinated HCP compared to unvaccinated individuals. The study found that each 2-fold increase in NAI titers reduced the risk of symptomatic infection by 42% against B/Phuket and 23% against B/Brisbane, independent of HAI titers. These findings suggest that NAI antibodies could be a strong correlate of protection against IBV, potentially offering broader protection if incorporated into influenza vaccines. However, the study's results are limited to the 2017-2018 season and focus on a specific population, which may affect generalizability.

title: Immunogenicity and safety of trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine in adults living with HIV compared with HIV-uninfected adults: a study from China

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the immunogenicity and safety of trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine (IIV3) in adults living with HIV and to provide evidence supporting influenza vaccination in this population in China.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This single-center, open-label comparative analysis was derived from a larger three-arm clinical study. It included 472 vaccinated participants, with 236 adults living with HIV (Group 1) and 236 age- and sex-comparable HIV-uninfected adults (Group 2).
analysis.methods: Blood samples were collected before and 28 days after vaccination for hemagglutination inhibition (HI) antibody testing against A(H1N1), A(H3N2), and B/Victoria strains. Safety was assessed by monitoring solicited and unsolicited adverse events (AEs) and serious adverse events (SAEs) during 6 months of follow-up.
analysis.main_results: A total of 489 participants were enrolled, including 237 in Group 1 and 252 in Group 2. At 28 days post-vaccination, seroconversion rates did not differ significantly between Group 1 and Group 2 for A(H1N1) (91.00% vs. 86.69%, P > 0.05), but significantly lower for A(H3N2) (49.50% vs. 89.52%) and B/Victoria (40.00% vs. 64.52%) (both P < 0.001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: HIV infection remained independently associated with reduced vaccine-induced immune responses for several strain-specific outcomes after multivariable adjustment, with associations particularly evident for A(H3N2).
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings support current recommendations for influenza vaccination in adults living with HIV, as IIV3 was generally safe and well tolerated.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was a single-center analysis, and the results may not be generalizable to other populations. The evidence is moderate due to the observational nature of the study and the lack of control for all potential confounding factors.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the immunogenicity and safety of trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine (IIV3) in adults living with HIV compared to HIV-uninfected adults in China. The research aimed to provide evidence for influenza vaccination in this population. A total of 489 participants were enrolled, with 237 in the HIV group and 252 in the uninfected group. At 28 days post-vaccination, seroconversion rates for A(H1N1) were similar between groups, but significantly lower for A(H3N2) and B/Victoria in the HIV group. HIV infection was independently associated with reduced immune responses to A(H3N2) after multivariable adjustment. The vaccine was generally safe and well tolerated, with most adverse events being mild. The study was a single-center analysis, which may limit generalizability, and the evidence is moderate due to the observational design and potential confounding factors.

title: Polyclonal breast milk–derived secretory IgA confers broad antiviral protection against multiple respiratory viruses

analysis.research_question_and_background: Passive immunization is an important tool for protecting individuals with primary immune deficiencies from infectious diseases and offers a rapid response strategy for protecting vulnerable populations, particularly during the interval between pathogen emergence and vaccine deployment.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Current approaches rely on intravenous delivery of IgG-enriched plasma or monoclonal antibodies, which limits accessibility, scalability, and effectiveness at mucosal surfaces, the primary entry point for respiratory viruses.
analysis.methods: Here, we tested LCTG-001, a polyclonal secretory IgA preparation derived from pooled human breast milk, to address these limitations.
analysis.main_results: LCTG-001 demonstrated broad antiviral activity against clinically relevant respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: LCTG-001 effectively recognized both group 1 and group 2 influenza A subtypes, including the highly pathogenic H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, and engaged nonneutralizing effector mechanisms such as neuraminidase inhibition and neutrophil activation.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: When administered intranasally, LCTG-001 conferred complete protection against influenza A challenge in both immunocompetent and antibody-deficient murine models, preventing morbidity and mortality through a transient early reduction in viral burden followed by sustained improvements in lung pathology and lung barrier integrity.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: These findings highlight the potential of breast milk-derived secretory IgA as a scalable, mucosa-targeted passive immunization strategy capable of addressing both endemic and emerging respiratory viral threats.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the potential of LCTG-001, a polyclonal secretory IgA preparation derived from human breast milk, as a passive immunization strategy against respiratory viruses. The research addresses the limitations of current approaches, which rely on intravenous delivery of IgG-enriched plasma or monoclonal antibodies. The study demonstrates that LCTG-001 has broad antiviral activity against respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus, including H5N1. When administered intranasally, it provides complete protection against influenza A in murine models, reducing viral burden and improving lung pathology. The findings suggest that breast milk-derived secretory IgA could be a scalable and mucosa-targeted solution for protecting vulnerable populations against both endemic and emerging respiratory viral threats. However, the study is limited to animal models, and further research is needed to confirm efficacy in humans.

title: Parental Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices Toward Influenza Vaccine Uptake Among Children in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia: A Cross-Sectional Study

analysis.research_question_and_background: Seasonal influenza is a major public health concern, particularly among children who are at high risk of infection and can transmit the virus to others.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A cross-sectional study was conducted among Saudi parents attending primary healthcare centers in Jeddah. Parents with at least one child aged six months or older were eligible.
analysis.methods: Data were collected using a validated self-administered Arabic questionnaire assessing knowledge, attitudes, awareness, perceived barriers, and vaccine uptake. Descriptive statistics and chi-square tests were used to examine associations, and binary logistic regression was performed to identify independent predictors of vaccine uptake.
analysis.main_results: A total of 308 parents participated. Influenza vaccine uptake was reported by 57.5% of participants. Nearly all participants (97.7%) demonstrated good knowledge, but the knowledge score was not significantly associated with vaccine uptake (p = 0.399). Parental attitude was a significant independent predictor (OR = 1.090, 95% CI: 1.033-1.149, p = 0.001). Education level was also significantly associated with uptake (p = 0.015), with lower-educated parents showing higher odds of vaccination compared to postgraduate-educated parents. Exposure to awareness campaigns was significantly associated with higher uptake (p < 0.001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Although most parents had good knowledge about influenza vaccination, this did not translate into consistent vaccination behavior. Parental attitudes and awareness campaign exposure were the main predictors of vaccine uptake.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Public health strategies should shift from broad factual dissemination to targeted, point-of-care counseling that addresses misconceptions about vaccine necessity and safety to improve influenza vaccination rates among children in Saudi Arabia.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report limitations of the study.

analysis.summary_en: This cross-sectional study in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, aimed to assess parental knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) toward influenza vaccine uptake among children. The study found that 57.5% of parents reported vaccinating their children, with nearly all (97.7%) demonstrating good knowledge. However, knowledge was not significantly associated with vaccine uptake. Parental attitude and exposure to awareness campaigns were significant predictors of vaccine uptake. The most reported barriers were the belief that vaccination was unnecessary and concerns about side effects. The study suggests that public health strategies should focus on targeted counseling to address misconceptions about vaccine necessity and safety. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the absence of reported limitations.

title: Shifts in acute respiratory pathogen epidemiology: an 8-year surveillance study in Hangzhou, China (2018–2025)

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to systematically characterize the epidemiological features of six key respiratory pathogens among acute respiratory tract infection (ARTI) cases in Hangzhou and evaluate the long-term impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on local pathogen dynamics.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was a retrospective surveillance study conducted in Hangzhou, China, from 2018 to 2025, analyzing 81,974 patients with ARTI. Cases were tested for influenza A virus (FluA), influenza B virus (FluB), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), adenovirus (ADV), Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP), and Chlamydia pneumoniae (CP).
analysis.methods: Positivity criteria followed the manufacturers' instructions for each respective assay. The co-infection rate was calculated, and statistical analysis was performed according to the pandemic stage, age, sex, season, and co-infection status.
analysis.main_results: Among 81,974 patients, 33,350 tested positive for pathogens, with an overall positivity rate of 40.68%. The positivity rates of FluA, FluB, and MP were significantly suppressed during the COVID-19 pandemic period (2020–2022) and then rebounded sharply in the post-pandemic period (2023–2025). In contrast, RSV, ADV, and CP showed persistent inhibition but had higher absolute case numbers than before the pandemic.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings reveal a dynamic shift in the epidemiology of respiratory pathogens, with FluA, FluB, and MP exhibiting a "revenge rebound" after the pandemic, while RSV, ADV, and CP remained inhibited but increased in absolute numbers. This pattern highlights the complex interplay between the pandemic and seasonal respiratory pathogens.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results suggest the need for a dynamic monitoring system to track changes in pathogen prevalence and implement targeted prevention and control measures during high-incidence seasons, particularly for FluA, FluB, and MP.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on a retrospective design, which may introduce bias, and the observed changes in positivity rates could be influenced by external factors such as public health interventions. The evidence is moderate due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study analyzed the epidemiology of six respiratory pathogens, including seasonal influenza viruses, in Hangzhou, China, over an 8-year period from 2018 to 2025. It found that the positivity rates of influenza A virus (FluA), influenza B virus (FluB), and Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP) were significantly suppressed during the COVID-19 pandemic but rebounded sharply afterward, forming a "revenge rebound" pattern. In contrast, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), adenovirus (ADV), and Chlamydia pneumoniae (CP) showed persistent inhibition but had higher absolute case numbers. The study highlights the need for dynamic monitoring and targeted prevention strategies during high-incidence seasons. However, the retrospective design and potential external influences limit the confidence in the findings, resulting in a moderate evidence assessment.

title: Clinical characteristics and exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality in pediatric severe viral encephalitis

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to identify clinical characteristics and exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality in pediatric severe viral encephalitis, addressing the need to better understand risk factors for this condition.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was conducted at the Department of Pediatrics, Anqing Municipal Hospital, from January 2023 to December 2025, involving 25 children diagnosed with severe viral encephalitis (SVE) and 50 children with mild encephalitis.
analysis.methods: Pathogen detection was conducted through multiplex PCR and/or serum viral IgM antibody testing. Univariate analyses and Firth-penalized logistic regression were used to explore factors associated with in-hospital mortality. Serum NSE was modeled as a continuous variable per 10 ng/mL increment. Neuroimaging and EEG were performed within 24 h of admission.
analysis.main_results: Among the 25 children with SVE, fever (76%), signs of elevated intracranial pressure (68%), and seizures (56%) were common, with four patients dying (16%). The SVE group had significantly longer hospital stays, higher seizure rates, lower GCS scores, higher proportions of abnormal EEG and neuroimaging abnormalities, and elevated serum NSE (all P < 0.05).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Neuroimaging abnormalities, seizures, EEG abnormalities, lower GCS score, and higher serum NSE were significantly associated with in-hospital mortality in the SVE group. The study highlights the importance of these factors in predicting severe outcomes.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Early recognition of these factors may aid in clinical risk assessment and improve management strategies for children with severe viral encephalitis.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential for selection bias. The evidence is moderate due to the observational nature of the study and the lack of randomized control.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates clinical characteristics and exploratory factors linked to in-hospital mortality in pediatric severe viral encephalitis (SVE). Conducted at Anqing Municipal Hospital from 2023 to 2025, it compares 25 SVE cases with 50 mild encephalitis cases. Pathogen detection involved multiplex PCR and IgM antibody testing, while univariate analyses and Firth-penalized logistic regression were used to assess risk factors. Results showed that fever, elevated intracranial pressure, and seizures were common in SVE, with four deaths (16%). The SVE group had longer hospital stays, higher seizure rates, lower GCS scores, and more abnormal EEG and neuroimaging findings. Neuroimaging abnormalities, seizures, EEG abnormalities, lower GCS scores, and higher serum NSE were significantly associated with mortality. The findings suggest these factors could aid in early risk assessment. However, the study's limitations include its retrospective design and potential selection bias, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

title: Identifying the immunocompetence markers at weaning to predict long-term vaccine response and persistence in pigs

analysis.research_question_and_background: Vaccination is a key strategy for controlling infectious disease in pigs, but the magnitude and persistence of vaccine-induced immunity vary among individuals.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Two vaccination trials were conducted in a cohort of 381 Large White pigs (MH, n=189; IAV, n=192).
analysis.methods: Long-term Ab status was defined at 118 days post-vaccination (dpv) using assay-specific thresholds, while Ab persistence was defined as the decline from the individual peak response at 28 or 35 dpv to 118 dpv.
analysis.main_results: Hematocrit, IgG, platelet count, and plateletcrit (PCT) were associated with positive long-term Ab status for both vaccines, whereas mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) and neutrophil percentage were associated with negative status. For persistence, higher vitamin D, -1 globulin concentration, platelet count, and PCT were consistently associated with persistent responses across vaccines, while MCHC and spectral absorbance traits were associated with non-persistence.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings indicate that early-life immune and physiological traits measured at weaning are associated with immunocompetence traits that contribute to variation in subsequent long-term vaccine antibody outcomes and responsiveness.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The identification of both shared and vaccine- or phenotype-specific predictors suggests that vaccine responsiveness reflects both general features of baseline immunocompetence and context-specific determinants.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Cross-validated accuracies ranged from 64.7% to 67.7%, indicating moderate predictive performance.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to identify immune and physiological markers at weaning that could predict long-term antibody status and persistence following vaccination against Mycoplasma hyopneumoniae (MH) and Influenza A virus (IAV) in pigs. The research found that hematocrit, IgG, platelet count, and plateletcrit (PCT) were associated with positive long-term antibody status, while MCHC and neutrophil percentage were linked to negative status. For antibody persistence, higher vitamin D, globulin concentration, platelet count, and PCT were consistently associated with persistent responses, whereas MCHC and spectral absorbance traits were linked to non-persistence. The results suggest that early-life immune and physiological traits are related to immunocompetence and can influence vaccine outcomes. However, the moderate predictive performance of the models indicates limitations in the strength of the evidence.

title: A prospective, comparative cohort analysis of influenza antibody waning in Michigan and Hong Kong during periods of low influenza circulation

analysis.research_question_and_background: Reduced influenza transmission during the COVID-19 pandemic prompted concern about waning of population immunity that could lead to subsequent surges in circulation. We compared longitudinal influenza antibody titers in Michigan and Hong Kong, two regions with reduced influenza transmission during the COVID-19 pandemic.
analysis.study_design_and_population: In two prospective cohort studies (HIVE, Michigan; EPI-HK, Hong Kong), we analyzed longitudinal serum samples collected from 2020 through 2023 from participants without influenza infection or vaccination.
analysis.methods: Sera were tested using hemagglutination inhibition assays (HAI) and microneutralization (MN) against vaccine strains. Two-year fold changes in titers were estimated using multivariable power-law models adjusted for age and baseline titer.
analysis.main_results: We analyzed 173 sera from 57 HIVE participants and 259 sera from 60 EPI-HK participants. Initial HAI geometric mean titers ranged from 12.3-123.4 in HIVE and 6.3-40.9 in EPI-HK. Among those with >1:40 baseline titers in HIVE, fold-change estimates indicated waning for H1N1 strains, including A/Brisbane (0.70 [95% CI: 0.56,0.86]), A/Idaho (0.40 [0.32,0.50]), and A/Michigan (0.43 [0.34,0.52]), while H3N2 and influenza B showed minimal or no waning. In EPI-HK, fold-change estimates demonstrated heterogeneous patterns by strain for H1N1, and waning for selected H3N2 strains, including A/Cambodia (0.44 [0.29,0.65]) and A/Singapore (0.48 [0.33,0.69]). MN results were consistent with HAI findings.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings suggest that population immunity was maintained for many strains despite reduced viral circulation, with waning occurring in particular strains and varying by population.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform surveillance strategies and vaccine development by highlighting strain-specific variations in antibody waning, which may affect future influenza outbreaks and public health interventions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on serum samples from participants without influenza infection or vaccination, and the evidence is moderate due to the observational nature of the cohort studies and potential confounding factors.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the waning of influenza antibody titers in Michigan and Hong Kong during periods of low influenza circulation. It compares longitudinal data from two cohort studies, HIVE and EPI-HK, analyzing serum samples collected between 2020 and 2023. The results show strain-specific variations in antibody waning, with significant declines observed for certain H1N1 strains but minimal or no waning for H3N2 and influenza B. The findings suggest that population immunity may be maintained for some strains despite reduced viral transmission, which has implications for surveillance and vaccine development. However, the study's observational design and reliance on participants without recent infection or vaccination limit the strength of the evidence, resulting in a moderate confidence assessment.
